title: Layered Architecture Fundamentals
summary: Why software separates into layers, how dependency direction between them is chosen, and the smells that show a layer boundary has already broken down.

slides.markdown:
Every codebase past a few hundred lines needs an answer to one question: **where does this piece of logic go?** Layering is the oldest and most common answer — split the system into horizontal slices, each responsible for one kind of concern, and let each slice depend only on the ones below it.

Done well, a layer boundary means a UI redesign never touches business rules, and swapping the database never touches either. Done badly — logic scattered across layers with no rule about direction — you get a codebase where changing one thing breaks three unrelated things.

This topic is the foundation the rest of the group builds on: dependency inversion, hexagonal architecture, and DDD are all refinements of the same layering idea.

slides.subTitle: Separating things that change for different reasons
slides.markdown:
The reason to layer isn't aesthetics — it's **rate of change**. A screen's layout changes every sprint as designers iterate. The rule for how a discount is calculated changes maybe twice a year. The choice of database changes maybe once in the system's lifetime.

If those three concerns live in the same function, every UI tweak risks touching the discount rule, and every discount tweak risks a typo in a SQL string. Layering groups code by **why it changes**, not by what feature it belongs to, so a change to one reason doesn't ripple into the others.

This is really Robert C. Martin's Single Responsibility Principle applied at the architectural scale rather than the class scale — a layer, like a class, should have one reason to change.

slides.subTitle: Presentation, business logic, data access
slides.markdown:
The textbook split has three layers, stacked so each one only talks to the layer directly below it:

- **Presentation** — HTTP controllers, CLI parsers, UI widgets. Translates the outside world's requests into calls the business layer understands, and formats results back out.
- **Business/domain logic** — the actual rules: pricing, eligibility, workflow state machines. This is the layer that would exist even if you rewrote the UI and swapped the database.
- **Data access** — SQL queries, ORM calls, file I/O, HTTP calls to other services. Knows how to persist and retrieve, and nothing about why.

A request flows top to bottom, a response flows bottom to top, and no layer skips a level or calls upward.

<<< Image: three horizontal bands labelled Presentation, Business/Domain Logic, and Data Access stacked top to bottom, with a downward arrow on the left showing an incoming request passing through all three and an upward arrow on the right showing the response passing back, plus a small crossed-out arrow showing Data Access is not allowed to call directly into Presentation >>>

The rule that makes layering work is not "put things in folders" — it's **dependency direction**. Presentation may import and call business logic. Business logic may import and call data access. Nothing goes the other way: data access never imports presentation, and business logic never imports presentation either.

Why this matters: the layer with the fewest dependents is the easiest to change safely, and the rule guarantees that's always the bottom layer's *consumers*, not the bottom layer's *internals*. Break the rule — let the data layer reach up into presentation to, say, format an error message for display — and now a UI change can break persistence code nobody thought to test.

In most languages this direction is enforceable: modules, packages, or `internal` visibility can make an upward import a compile error rather than a convention someone forgets.

slides.subTitle: And the smell of logic in the wrong layer
slides.markdown:
A quick test for which layer a piece of code belongs in: **would it survive a total UI rewrite? A total database swap?**

- "Format the price as `$12.99`" survives neither — it's presentation.
- "An order under $50 doesn't qualify for free shipping" survives both — it's business logic, full stop, regardless of whether it runs in a web handler or a database trigger.
- "Insert this row, retrying on a unique-constraint violation" survives a UI rewrite but not a database swap — it's data access.

The smell to watch for is business logic **described in terms of its current layer** — a controller with an `if` chain implementing pricing rules, or a SQL `CASE` expression encoding eligibility. The rule itself doesn't care which layer runs it; the moment it's written using that layer's vocabulary (HTTP status codes, SQL syntax), it has quietly moved in.

| | Everything in one function | Layered |
|---|---|---|
| **Adding a second UI (e.g. a CLI alongside the web app)** | Copy-paste the business rules into the new entry point | Reuse the business layer unchanged |
| **Swapping Postgres for DynamoDB** | Rewrite scattered SQL calls wherever they appear | Rewrite one data-access module |
| **Unit testing the discount rule** | Requires a running HTTP server and a database | Call the business function directly with plain inputs |
| **Onboarding a new engineer** | Must read the whole function to find the one rule that changed | Go straight to the layer that owns that concern |

The one-file version isn't wrong for a 50-line script — it's wrong once the system has more than one reason to change, which is most systems past a prototype.

slides.subTitle: Business logic living in the presentation layer
slides.markdown:
The most common layering violation: a controller method that parses the request, validates it, applies business rules, calls the database directly, and formats the response, all in one 80-line function.

This happens gradually — a small `if` check added to a handler "just this once" becomes the permanent home for a rule, because the handler is where the request already is and adding one more line feels free. Six months later the same eligibility rule is duplicated across three controllers (web, mobile API, admin panel) with three subtly different bugs.

The fix is mechanical: any conditional that references business concepts ("is this order eligible", "has this user's trial expired") gets extracted into a business-layer function that the controller merely calls. The controller's job shrinks back to translating HTTP in and HTTP out.

slides.subTitle: The data layer contaminating business logic
slides.markdown:
The mirror-image mistake: passing an ORM-mapped row object (a Django model, a JPA `@Entity`, an ActiveRecord instance) straight into business logic and treating it as the domain object.

The problem shows up later, not immediately. The ORM entity carries persistence baggage — lazy-loaded relations that throw if accessed outside a database session, column names that don't match the business vocabulary, framework annotations. Business logic written against it silently depends on being inside an active database transaction, and a rule that should be a pure function (given these inputs, is this order eligible?) becomes untestable without a real database connection.

The fix is a thin mapping step: load the ORM entity in the data layer, convert it to a plain object the business layer owns the shape of, and never let the ORM type cross that boundary.

A common misconception is that layering is only about microservice boundaries or separate deployables. It applies just as much **inside a single monolith, inside a single module, even inside a single class file** — the enforcement mechanism differs, but the direction rule doesn't.

A well-organized monolith has the same three-layer split as folders or packages within one repository and one deployed binary: `handlers/`, `domain/`, `repository/`, with the same import rule (`domain/` never imports `handlers/`). Nothing here requires a network hop or a separate process.

This matters because "we're not doing microservices" is sometimes used to justify skipping layering entirely. The two decisions are independent: you can have a beautifully layered monolith or a tangled mess of microservices where each service itself has no internal boundaries.

slides.sectionTitle: Where layering runs out of road
slides.markdown:
Plain layering has a known weak spot: it says business logic must not depend on data access's *code*, but by convention the business layer often still imports the data layer's interface — meaning the direction is right but business logic still can't run without knowing the data layer exists.

That gap is exactly what the next topic in this group closes. Dependency inversion keeps the same three concerns but flips who defines the contract between them, so the business layer can be tested and understood with zero knowledge of what database, if any, sits underneath it.

For now, the takeaway to carry forward: layering is a rule about **dependency direction between concerns that change at different rates**, enforced structurally, not just followed by convention.
